UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
) 
) 
) 
)
 
 
Docket No. ER26-1479-000 
MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND LIMITED ANSWER  
OF THE INDUSTRIAL CUSTOMER ORGANIZATIONS AND AMTRAK 
 
Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC” 
or “Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 the PJM Industrial Customer Coalition 
(“PJMICC”), the Industrial Energy Consumers of America (“IECA”), the American Forest and 
Paper Association (“AF&PA”) (collectively, “Industrials”), and the National Railroad Passenger 
Corporation (“Amtrak”) hereby request leave to submit this Motion for Leave to Answer and 
Limited Answer (“Limited Answer”) to the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners’ (“Transmission 
Owners”) Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer (“April 24 Motion/Answer”).2 
I. 
MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER 
The Industrials/Amtrak respectfully request leave to file this Limited Answer, which is 
only being filed in response to the unauthorized April 24 Answer of the Transmission Owners. 
Rule 213(a)(2) generally prohibits answers to answers unless such answers have been authorized 
by the decisional authority.3 However, the Commission exercises its discretion to grant motions 
for leave to submit answers when doing so will clarify the issues, assist in the Commission’s 
 
1 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212 and 385.213. 
2 Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer of the Indicated Transmission Owners, Docket No. ER26-1479-000 (Apr. 
24, 2026). The Answer was filed on April 24, 2026, in response to various protests and comments on PJM 
Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) 60-Day Compliance Filing in the above-captioned proceeding. 60-Day Compliance 
Filing for Co-Located Load Related Revisions to Open Access Transmission Tariff to Comply with Commission 
Order in Docket No. EL25-49, et al, Docket No. ER26-1479-000 (Feb. 23, 2026) (“Compliance Filing”). 
3 18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(2).

2 
 
decision-making processes, or otherwise ensure an accurate and complete record.4  
Procedurally, the Industrials/Amtrak question the Transmission Owners’ decision to file 
the April 24 Motion/Answer well over 30 days after protests and comments were filed and after 
the record had already been developed.5 The Industrials/Amtrak provide this Limited Answer 
solely in response to the late-filed April 24 Motion/Answer, to assist the Commission in its 
decision-making process.  
Of note, the Industrials/Amtrak are representative of the entities who will be most directly 
(sometimes existentially) affected by the FERC’s determinations in this proceeding. While many 
parties have weighed in on PJM’s proposed retail Behind-the-Meter Generation (“BTMG”) rules, 
it is the industrial and institutional sectors whose future survival and growth are at issue in this 
docket.6 These customers serve as the backbone of American manufacturing, health care, and 
transportation services. Therefore, if the Commission accepts the April 24 Motion/Answer, the 
Industrials/Amtrak respectfully ask the Commission to accept this Limited Answer, as well. 
II. 
LIMITED ANSWER 
A. 
The Transmission Owners’ discussion of the Retail Threshold fails to address 
any arguments for a Retail Threshold of 200 MW or above and fails to address 
evidence showing the damage of a too-low Retail Threshold to resource 
adequacy, economic growth, and cost-causation. 
In the April 24 Motion/Answer, the Transmission Owners address the materiality threshold 
for application of retail BTMG rules (“Retail Threshold”), contending that “the 50 MW threshold 
 
4 See, e.g., PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 145 FERC ¶ 61,035, at P 32 (2013); Wisconsin Pub. Serv. Corp., 144 FERC 
¶ 61,093, at P 27 (2013); Iberdrola Renewables, Inc., 137 FERC ¶ 61,185, at P 17 (2011); Virginia Elec. and Power 
Co., 125 FERC ¶ 61,391, at P 26 (2008). 
5 18 CFR § 385.213(d). 
6 As set forth in the Joint Protest and Comments of Industrial Customer Organizations and Amtrak, Docket No. ER26-
1479-000 (Mar. 16, 2026) (“Industrials/Amtrak Protest”) and the Affidavit of James R. Dauphinais (“Dauphinais 
Affidavit”) attached thereto, traditional customers with on-site generation are facing enormous challenges that, 
depending on the final order in this docket, will render some of that on-site generation uneconomic. See, e.g., 
Dauphinais Affidavit at P 17. PJM also recognized the danger of units closing. See Compliance Filing at 12-15.

3 
 
strikes the appropriate balance between allowing continued use of Retail BTMG and appropriate 
limitations to ensure reliability.” The Transmission Owners further state:  
PJM reasonably selected 50 MW because that threshold aligns with the PJM 
Board’s definition of large load additions, preserves existing treatment for smaller 
and longstanding Retail BTMG arrangements, and avoids sweeping in retail 
customers whose grid impacts are comparatively limited.7 
 
The Transmission Owners fail to substantiate their newly articulated position with any 
evidence. Despite extensive information provided in the Industrials/Amtrak’s Protest and in other 
filings in this docket as to why a Retail Threshold of 200 MW is critical, the Transmission Owners 
do not address any of these arguments.  
In contrast, the Industrials/Amtrak provided an extensive affidavit demonstrating that 
traditional customers substantially larger than 50 MW reliably operate with retail BTMG. These 
are the factories that produce paper, pharmaceuticals, and steel; and the trains that carry thousands 
of passengers every day across the PJM footprint and beyond. Many of them are qualifying 
facilities (“QF”) under the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act of 1978 (“PURPA”), subject to 
efficiency standards (and, for non-cogeneration QFs, size limits). Some are operationally limited 
in what they can draw from the grid. These customers’ reliable operation of BTMG supports the 
cost-causation basis for the actual use approach of BTMG. 
The Industrials/Amtrak also demonstrated that load under 200 MW—particularly 
industrial and institutional load—is not driving today’s reliability challenges.8 The historical 
reliance on BTMG rules is supported by the Commission’s affirmations that actual use was the 
operative principle. The Commission was and is correct. Actual use should remain the operative 
principle, with the caveat that certain considerations must be made for loads that create substantial 
 
7 April 24 Motion/Answer at 2. 
8 Industrials/Amtrak Protest at 14-15.

4 
 
reliability risk. As the Commission stated, BTMG rules should (and will) be maintained; the 
question is to what extent. The Industrials/Amtrak Protest provided concrete, sound reasons why 
PJM’s proposed 50 MW is too low; they also provided information on the harm that will result if 
50 MW is selected, including loss of generation resources, which would heighten existing resource 
adequacy challenges.9 However, these facts have not been addressed (let alone refuted) by the 
Transmission Owners, who simply opine that 50 MW “strikes the appropriate balance.” In 
contrast, the Industrials/Amtrak have presented compelling evidence that a 200 MW or greater 
Retail Threshold aligns with the Commission’s directive in the December 18, 2025, Order.10 
B. 
The Retail Threshold should be based on load, not generator size.   
The April 24 Motion/Answer also endorses PJM’s proposal that the Retail Threshold be 
based on generator nameplate rating, stating: “The Order expressly directed PJM to propose a new 
MW threshold for Retail BTMG and explained that such a threshold should reduce the reliability 
 
9 In their Protest, the Industrials/Amtrak explained why PJM’s alternative Retail Threshold of at least 200 MW is 
superior to the main proposal of 50 MW, including: 
(1) A 200 MW Retail Threshold maintains incentives that bolster resource adequacy and grid 
efficiency, thereby avoiding inefficient transmission investment. 
(2) A 200 MW Retail Threshold preserves the focus on reliability challenges caused by super-
sized load, while avoiding economically devastating outcomes for manufacturing, 
institutional and transportation facilities. 
(3) A 200 MW Retail Threshold avoids major administrative disincentives to operate on-site 
generation by avoiding the need to force existing retail customers into new and unfamiliar 
regulation, requiring them to become FERC-regulated public utilities, secure PJM membership, 
and undertake related credit and risk requirements.   
(4) A 200 MW Retail Threshold aligns with regulatory logic that identifies various “tiers” of 
large load.  
(5) A 200 MW Retail Threshold avoids burdening PJM with a significant number of studies 
for existing generators (for generator deactivations or for BTMG that becomes Co-Located 
Generation). 
(6) A 200 MW Retail Threshold de-emphasizes grandfathering and emphasizes stable rules for 
customers, a more durable approach. 
(7) A 200 MW Retail Threshold respects the importance of onshoring manufacturing, 
consistent with federal and state economic development goals.  
Industrials/Amtrak Protest at 25; see also id. at 23-33. 
10 Order on Show Cause Proceeding, Directing Compliance Filings, Establishing Paper Hearing, and Granting In Part 
and Denying In Part Complaint, Docket Nos. EL25-49-000, EL25-49-001, AD24-11-000, EL25-20-000 
(“Consolidated Dockets”) (Dec. 18, 2025) (“Order”).

5 
 
and resource adequacy risks posed by large Retail BTMG, while allowing smaller customers to 
continue netting in a transparent and not unduly discriminatory manner.”11 
However, this argument misstates the Commission’s directive, as the Commission did not 
propose a generation-based threshold and did not limit netting to a particular customer type (e.g., 
“smaller customers”). Rather, the December 18, 2026, Order directs PJM to “propose a new MW 
threshold for the amount of load at a particular electrical location that Network Customers may 
net by using BTMG.”12 The language of the Order indicates that retail netting should continue at 
all retail electrical locations but only up to the Retail Threshold that the Commission ultimately 
approves.13 Unfortunately, PJM’s proposal is based on generation size, meaning that if generation 
is sized above the Retail Threshold, the electrical location would be entirely disqualified from 
netting; it also incorporates an “all-or-nothing” design.  
As explained in the Industrials/Amtrak’s Protest, PJM’s design choice is contrary to a plain 
reading of the Order, creates an unfortunate economic “cliff” effect, and marks an unjustified shift 
from the current definition of BTMG (despite the Order directing that BTMG rules be 
maintained).14 PJM’s proposal would produce radically different results for an entity just below 
the threshold versus one just above, creating a paralysis of investment for growing American 
companies. In contrast, the Commission’s original directive is reasonable because it avoids an “all-
or-nothing” design that disincentivizes growth and investment.   
 
11 April 24 Motion/Answer at 2-3. 
12 Order at P 221 (emphasis added). See also Order at P 179 (“we direct PJM to maintain the current BTMG rules for 
customers that fall below a new MW materiality threshold for the amount of load at a particular electrical location that 
Network Customers may net using BTMG”). 
13 Paragraph 221 of the Order places no limiting language on which Network Customers or electrical locations may 
“reduce their transmission charges in a transparent, not unduly discriminatory fashion.”   
14 See Order at P 221. The Dauphinais Affidavit provides additional reasons why a generation-based Retail Threshold 
is inappropriate. Dauphinais Affidavit at PP 55-60.

6 
 
On a related note, while the Industrials/Amtrak offered substantial explanation and 
arguments concerning the unique role of QFs in the regulatory framework, the April 24 
Motion/Answer does not address these issues or offer any insight into how PURPA regulations 
should apply in the context of retail BTMG rules, despite the fact that many QFs, particularly 
cogeneration QFs, produce above 50 MW. The Industrials/Amtrak continue to urge the 
Commission to ensure QFs have access to back-up power as required by law.15 
C. 
Regulatory certainty and legally durable rules are essential for investment. 
While grandfathering rules should be broad to avoid unnecessary economic 
harm, they should be complemented by a Retail Threshold that provides 
certainty for future growth. 
The Industrials/Amtrak appreciate the Transmission Owners’ recognition of the 
importance of robust grandfathering to protect existing retail customers who would be financially 
harmed by the elimination of the BTMG operations.16 In particular, the Industrials/Amtrak agree 
that the “existing contract” exception should be construed broadly and, when in doubt, the 
grandfathering provision should be applied favorably to the existing customer.17 New or expanded 
facility operations that have made material progress should be included in applicable 
grandfathering provisions. 
While the Industrials/Amtrak appreciate the Transmission Owners’ robust support for 
grandfathering provisions, reliance solely on grandfathering provisions adds complexity and 
uncertainty—two enemies of investment. For example: 
 Does a factory remain grandfathered if it needs to add one new production line in 
the future, increasing its demand by 1 MW? Can it make that investment without 
 
15 18 C.F.R. § 292.305(b)-(c). Subsection (c) states, in relevant part, “The rate for sales of back-up power or 
maintenance power … [s]hall not be based upon an assumption (unless supported by factual data) that forced outages 
or other reductions in electric output by all qualifying facilities on an electric utility's system will occur simultaneously, 
or during the system peak, or both.”  
16 Answer at 3-4. 
17 Id. at 3.

7 
 
triggering a transition to Co-Located Load status, with all the protective equipment 
requirements and other operational requirements? 
 
 If a large hospital system operating combined heat and power (“CHP”) is sold to a 
different parent company or completes a merger, does grandfathering remain 
intact? 
 
 Do facilities adding a new resource type lose grandfathering status? For example, 
does a facility seeking to complement its on-site resources with battery storage lose 
its grandfathering status altogether? 
 
 When do large industrial companies who are making deliberate, methodical long-
term plans (e.g., 5, 10, 15, or 20 years) for electrification have to abandon their 
BTMG status and begin the involved process of becoming Co-Located Load? 
 
While the Commission may be able to address some of these scenarios, they create a 
regulatory minefield for industrial and institutional retail customers who may be making energy-
efficient investments. Some manufacturers in the PJM region intend to expand through a 
methodical, well-thought-out process (and without the speed-to-market demands that many data 
centers now present). Over-reliance on grandfathering rules will make this process more daunting 
for decision makers who must be accountable to their shareholders and stakeholders. 
Unfortunately, the risk that a facility may not be grandfathered will chill and disincentivize 
investment.  
Most industrial and institutional entities providing critical goods and services must work 
vigilantly to remain viable in a competitive global economy. Investments are made deliberately 
and with care. These customers must have a reasonable degree of certainty about their investments, 
including regulatory certainty. While grandfathering helps to avoid short-term closure of BTMG 
units (and potentially closure of some factories), it does not offer a roadmap for growth for existing 
customers who wish to expand and invest. Robust grandfathering rules should be complemented 
by a reasonable Retail Threshold of at least 200 MW of load, including all QFs who have rights to 
cost-based back-up power (which retail BTMG status provides) under PURPA and its 
implementing regulations.

8 
 
III. 
CONCLUSION & REQUEST FOR RELIEF 
The Industrials/Amtrak respectfully request that the Commission accept their Limited 
Answer above; reject PJM’s Compliance Filing, consistent with their Protest and Comments filed 
on March 16, 2026; and direct PJM to file a new compliance filing, consistent with the 
Industrials/Amtrak’s Protest and Comments. 
 
 
 
 
 
Respectfully submitted, 
 
By: 
/s/ Susan E. Bruce
